 AI mosquito trap could speed dengue surveillance in Florida
 Sunday, 15 November 2026, 18:55 
 Photo source: Fox News 
 A system developed by University of South Florida researchers identified mosquito species with more than 98% accuracy in laboratory tests. Its developers are preparing to validate the technology in the field in Hillsborough County. 
 Florida is dealing with its largest dengue outbreak in decades. The Florida Department of Health’s latest available weekly surveillance report recorded 407 locally acquired cases in Hillsborough County in 2026, the county’s largest outbreak on record. Statewide, officials had reported 524 locally acquired cases through October 31. These cases were contracted from mosquitoes in the area, rather than during overseas travel.
 This is reported by Fox News .
 On November 13, Hillsborough County said it had extended its state of local emergency through November 19 as mosquito-control crews increased aerial and ground treatments. County officials said surveillance continued to detect dengue virus activity in neighborhoods across the area. Dengue can cause high fever, severe headaches and intense muscle pain, and may lead to life-threatening complications in serious cases.
 Advertisement 
 How the trap works
 The system was developed by Digitomy, a startup founded by University of South Florida researchers Ryan Carney, an associate professor, and Sriram Chellappan, a professor. Their research on the system dates to 2018. It is designed to help mosquito-control teams identify captured insects without waiting for specialists to examine them under a microscope, a process that can take two to three days.
 A light or bait attracts mosquitoes into the trap, where a small fan draws them inside. After they land on a sticky pad, two built-in cameras photograph them. AI compares the images with a database to identify the species. The system can also identify whether a mosquito is male or female and whether it has recently fed on blood. Female mosquitoes bite people and can transmit diseases.
 The researchers say the system identified mosquito species with more than 98% accuracy in laboratory testing. Digitomy aims to use AI and cloud computing to provide identification on the same day and display results on a mapping dashboard for mosquito-control teams. The trap identifies species capable of carrying disease; it does not confirm that a mosquito is infected with dengue. That would still require laboratory testing.
 Testing and plans
 The system has been tested at the University of South Florida and with the Anastasia Mosquito Control District in St. Johns County, which includes St. Augustine. Digitomy is preparing for field validation with Hillsborough County. The researchers have also added trap information to a private layer of their Global Mosquito Observations Dashboard, which includes more than half a million citizen-science reports. The dashboard can combine automated trap data with observations from the public.
 Digitomy’s system could complement an early-warning system Carney developed for dengue and West Nile virus. The researchers say faster information could help officials respond sooner, although detecting mosquitoes early does not guarantee an outbreak can be prevented.
 The startup is working with the University of South Florida’s Technology Transfer office to license the AI identification system to established mosquito-trap manufacturers. The university has not announced a consumer launch date or retail price. Digitomy received a $25,000 grant from the USF Research Foundation’s Bull Ring Accelerator during summer 2026 to help accelerate licensing and commercialization of university-developed technology. The team is also developing an online platform where mosquito-control professionals and the public can practice identifying species using images and AI-generated feedback.
 For now, the source recommends removing standing water from outdoor containers, using EPA-registered insect repellent and wearing long sleeves and pants to reduce exposed skin when spending time outdoors.
